hints: Think what bond joins amino acids in E and what small molecule must be added to break it.
walkthrough:
Spot the link to break**
Look at E and you will see two $\text{-CO-NH-}$ peptide links joining three amino acid residues. Hydrolysis means adding $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ across each $\text{C-N}$ bond to give free $\text{-COOH}$ and $\text{-NH}_2$ (in ionic form). Amides are quite unreactive, so you need vigorous conditions.

Choose a complete set of conditions**
Pick one reliable route and give all three parts: reagent, aqueous and dilute, plus heating. For acid: dilute aqueous $\text{HCl}$, heat under reflux. For alkali: dilute aqueous $\text{NaOH}$, heat under reflux. For enzyme: protease in water at about $37^{\circ}\text{C}$. Remember your choice because it controls the ionic form in (a)(ii).

Final answer: Heat under reflux with dilute aqueous $\text{HCl}$ (or $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$). Alternative: heat under reflux with dilute aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ / $\text{OH}^{-}$, or warm with protease enzyme in water at $30^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $40^{\circ}\text{C}$.

hints: Split E at the two peptide $\text{C-N}$ bonds and write each fragment as $\text{H}_2\text{N-CH(R)-COOH}$, identifying R as $\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ and $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$.
Adjust $\text{-NH}_2$ to $\text{-NH}_3^{+}$ in acid, and $\text{-COOH}$ to $\text{-COO}^{-}$ in alkali, including the extra $\text{COOH}$ side chain of glutamic acid.
walkthrough:
Cut out the three residues**
Imagine adding water across each $\text{-CO-NH-}$. The left residue has R = $\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, so it is isoleucine. The middle residue has R = $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, so it is serine. The right residue has R = $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$, so it is glutamic acid.

Put them in the correct ionic form**
This is where many students slip. If you chose acid hydrolysis, everything basic is protonated: $\text{-NH}_2$ becomes $\text{-NH}_3^{+}$ and every $\text{-COO}^{-}$ becomes $\text{-COOH}$. So glutamic acid is drawn with two neutral $\text{COOH}$ groups plus $\text{NH}_3^{+}$. If you had chosen alkali, you would do the opposite: $\text{-NH}_3^{+}$ becomes $\text{-NH}_2$ and every $\text{-COOH}$ becomes $\text{-COO}^{-}$.

Draw cleanly**
Draw central $\text{C}$ with four bonds: $\text{NH}_3^{+}$, $\text{COOH}$, $\text{H}$ and R group. Check you have three separate amino acids, not still joined, and that charges balance for your chosen conditions.

Final answer: For acid hydrolysis ($\text{H}^{+}$, reflux): $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)CH(NH}_3^{+}\text{)COOH}$ [isoleucine], $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH(NH}_3^{+}\text{)COOH}$ [serine], $\text{HOOCCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH(NH}_3^{+}\text{)COOH}$ [glutamic acid, both $\text{COOH}$ groups protonated]. All $\text{NH}_2$ as $\text{NH}_3^{+}$, all $\text{COO}^{-}$ as $\text{COOH}$.

hints: Scan E for polar $\text{C=O}$, $\text{N-H}$ and $\text{O-H}$ bonds that give permanent partial charges even without H-bonding.
Look for $\text{H}$ attached to $\text{N}$ or $\text{O}$ as H-bond donors, and lone pairs on $\text{C=O}$, $\text{-OH}$ or $\text{-COO}^{-}$ as H-bond acceptors.
Remember E is shown with full charges $\text{-COO}^{-}$ and $\text{-NH}_3^{+}$, so think what attraction occurs between oppositely charged groups on different molecules.
walkthrough:
Permanent dipole-dipole from polar bonds**
E is full of $\text{C}^{\delta+}=\text{O}^{\delta-}$, $\text{N}^{\delta-}-\text{H}^{\delta+}$ and $\text{O}^{\delta-}-\text{H}^{\delta+}$. When two E molecules line up, the $\delta^{+}$ end of one polar group attracts the $\delta^{-}$ end of another. For example, the $\delta^{+}$ $\text{H}$ in $\text{NH}$ attracts the $\delta^{-}$ $\text{O}$ in $\text{C=O}$.

Hydrogen bonds as the strong special case**
Hydrogen bonding needs $\text{H}$ bonded to $\text{N}$ or $\text{O}$ plus a lone pair on $\text{N}$ or $\text{O}$. E has donors: peptide $\text{NH}$, alcohol $\text{OH}$, carboxylic acid $\text{OH}$, $\text{NH}_3^{+}$. It has acceptors: $\text{C=O}$ of amide and acid, $\text{OH}$ and $\text{COO}^{-}$. A typical pair is $\text{N-H}$ donor with $\text{C=O}$ acceptor.

Ionic attraction from the zwitterion-like ends**
Notice the diagram already shows $\text{-COO}^{-}$ at one end and $\text{-NH}_3^{+}$ at the other. In solution these full charges on neighbouring molecules attract strongly. That is ionic bonding between molecules, much stronger than dipole forces. London forces from the alkyl $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9$ side chain can also be quoted but the three required types are dipole-dipole, H-bond and ionic.

Final answer: Permanent dipole-dipole: between $\delta^{+}$ on e.g. $\text{NH}$ / $\text{OH}$ and $\delta^{-}$ on e.g. $\text{C=O}$ / $\text{COOH}$ / $\text{OH}$. Hydrogen bonding: H-bond donor $\text{N-H}$ / $\text{O-H}$ with lone pair acceptor on $\text{C=O}$ / $\text{COOH}$ / $\text{OH}$ / $\text{CONH}$. Ionic bonding: between $\text{NH}_3^{+}$ on one molecule and $\text{COO}^{-}$ on another.

hints: Think what two functional groups must react to make an amide link, and how one molecule could contain both of them.
walkthrough:
Design a self-reacting monomer**
A polyamide link $\text{-CO-NH-}$ forms from $\text{-COOH}$ plus $\text{-NH}_2$ with loss of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$. If one molecule carries an amine at one end and a carboxylic acid (or acyl chloride) at the other, it can join head to tail with itself repeatedly. The simplest is aminoethanoic acid, $\text{H}_2\text{N-CH}_2\text{-COOH}$, but any $\text{H}_2\text{N-R-COOH}$ is accepted.
Final answer: Any molecule containing both $\text{NH}_2$ and $\text{COOH}$ (or $\text{COCl}$), e.g. $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{COOH}$ or $\text{H}_2\text{N(CH}_2\text{)}_5\text{COOH}$.

hints: Recall a polyester needs a diol plus a dioic acid (or diacyl chloride) to make repeated ester links.
Count carbons: the two monomers together minus water lost must leave only four carbons in the repeat unit, so think how many carbons each monomer can contribute.
Draw the simplest 2-carbon diol with two $\text{-OH}$ groups.
Draw the matching 2-carbon diacid with two $\text{-COOH}$ groups (or two $\text{-COCl}$ groups) and name both compounds systematically.
walkthrough:
Work backwards from four carbons**
A polyester repeat unit contains residues from both monomers. To total four carbons, the simplest split is 2 + 2. So you need a 2-carbon diol and a 2-carbon diacid.

Draw the diol**
The 2-carbon diol is $\text{HO-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-OH}$. Its systematic name is ethane-1,2-diol (ethylene glycol). Both $\text{OH}$ groups will form ester links.

Draw the diacid**
The 2-carbon diacid is $\text{HOOC-COOH}$, where the two carbons are both carboxyl carbons directly joined. Its name is ethanedioic acid (oxalic acid). The diacyl chloride $\text{ClOC-COCl}$, ethanedioyl chloride, is also accepted and is more reactive.

Check the repeat unit**
Join them: $\text{-O-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-O-CO-CO-}$ plus $2\text{H}_2\text{O}$ lost. Count carbons in the chain: two from the diol plus two from the diacid equals four, exactly as required.

Final answer: $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, ethane-1,2-diol; $\text{HOOC-COOH}$ (or $\text{ClOC-COCl}$), ethanedioic acid (or ethanedioyl chloride). Repeat unit $\text{-O-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-O-CO-CO-}$ contains four carbons.
